mainText:
If you only remember one thing today, remember this. An anonymous frontier A I model with a one million token context window has been running free for a week, and no lab will admit building it. The forensics point to China.

Section one. The model nobody will claim.

This is at the top of both your Rundown and your A I Collective this morning. A stealth model called Ox Alpha appeared on Open Router on August twentieth. It has a context window of just over one million tokens. It takes text, images, and video. It calls tools. And the preview price is zero dollars. No lab has put its name on it.

Independent sleuths went to work. They studied tokenizer quirks, and, memorably, emoji frequency. The leading theory is that this is Zhipu A I's unreleased G L M five point three, probably a fast variant. Zhipu has not confirmed. And one lab is reportedly handing out one hundred trillion free tokens a day to keep the test running.

Worth noting, this is the fifth time this year that an anonymous alpha model has surfaced on a routing platform, run free for a week or two, and then been claimed as a launch.

Why it matters. Free stealth launches are now a standard way to go to market. And when the strongest frontier candidate of the week turns out to be Chinese, the export control conversation changes shape.

Section two. Nvidia goes to orbit.

Your Rundown leads with the Space X and Nvidia partnership moving from announcement to actual hardware. Nvidia supplies the computing payload for Starmind A I One. That's a satellite designed to run A I workloads in space, on next generation Rubin graphics chips and Vera processors. It runs on solar power, and connects back to Earth by high bandwidth laser links.

Musk projects that Space X A I computing capacity will pass two gigawatts by the end of this year, and approach ten gigawatts by the end of next year.

Why it matters. If computing in orbit actually works, the energy and water fights that are currently stalling data centers on the ground get an escape hatch. And Nvidia holds an exclusive chip role in it.

Section three. The gaps in Nvidia's five hundred billion dollar pitch.

This comes from your Information. Nvidia lined up half a dozen financial giants, including Blackstone, Apollo, and Goldman Sachs, to finance five hundred billion dollars of A I infrastructure purchases. The piece walks through what that structure actually covers, what it doesn't, and where the funding assumptions get thin.

Why it matters. The A I buildout is increasingly a credit story, not a chip story. And credit stories break differently than technology ones do.

Section four. The watermarking era begins.

This is your E U A I Act newsletter, issue one hundred and nine. Anthropic has set out how it will mark Claude's text output, as the A I Act's transparency obligations take effect. Enforcement started on August second. Chatbots must disclose that they are not human. Deepfakes must be labelled. And A I generated content needs machine readable marks. Experts in this issue push back on the claim that watermarking degrades A I writing quality.

The rules for high risk systems got pushed back. December of twenty twenty seven for standalone systems, and August of twenty twenty eight for embedded ones.

Why it matters. You're in communications. Disclosure and provenance labels are about to become a routine part of every A I assisted communication you or your clients ship.

Section five. Chips, and the offshore loophole.

Two threads are converging here. Bloomberg reports that a U S agency is systematically reviewing how Chinese A I firms access Nvidia chips overseas. Chiefly by renting computing power in third countries. This follows a run of Chinese technical breakthroughs. A notice from the Bureau of Industry and Security back on May thirty first already extended licensing requirements to companies headquartered in restricted jurisdictions, even when the entity itself sits somewhere else.

Meanwhile, your Recode China A I digest reports Nvidia chips getting a green light in Beijing, alongside Unitree's blockbuster public debut.

Why it matters. Export controls on shipments do not control access. And rented computing power is the gap that everyone is now looking at.

Section six. The data center pause.

This is from your Tech Policy Press. Jurisdictions across the United States are pressing pause on new data centers. New York went first. That's the top of the news. Your full briefing is in the recording.
